title: "file10.txt" sorts before "file2.txt"
assumption: Sorting a list of filenames (or any strings with embedded numbers) alphabetically also puts them in numeric order for the number part.

input.description: A directory listing, a set of uploaded files (page-01.jpg, page-02.jpg, ..., page-10.jpg), or any auto-numbered set of names sorted with a plain string comparison.

what_goes_wrong: A plain sort returns ["file1.txt", "file10.txt", "file2.txt"] — "file10.txt" is placed between "file1.txt" and "file2.txt", because standard string comparison never looks at the embedded number as a number at all.
why: String comparison walks the two strings character by character until it finds a difference. "file1" and "file10" and "file2" all share the prefix "file"; comparing position by position, "1" < "2" decides "file10" < "file2" before the comparison ever reaches the second digit of "10" — the strings are compared as sequences of characters, not parsed into a text part and a numeric part the way a human reads them. This is true identically in Python and JavaScript, because both default to the same kind of character-by-character comparison; neither treats a run of digits as a single unit unless you tell it to.
fix: Use a "natural sort": split each string into alternating text/number runs and compare the number runs numerically (JavaScript has this built into localeCompare's {numeric: true} option; Python's standard library has no equivalent and needs a hand-written key function, e.g. splitting on digit runs with re.split and converting the digit groups to int).

sources.title: Unicode Technical Standard #10: Unicode Collation Algorithm

test_cases.note: their_function(a, b) as a natural-order "a sorts before b" test should return false: file2 belongs before file10. Plain `a < b` returns true, which is the bug.
